selection_rule: top-k species by (n_distinct_proposers, n_members, stable sha256); representative = member with smallest sha256(pid)

selected.name: Curiosity gap
selected.instruction: Score high when the headline withholds key information the reader must click to resolve ('this photo', 'wasn't about Manafort', 'something in room'). Score low when the headline states its own conclusion.
selected.rationale: Withheld referents drive click-through regardless of topic.

selected.name: Explicit emotion word
selected.instruction: Headline contains emotion terms (fear, outrage, love, demons, gross). Scores high when emotion is the story; not for neutral reporting
selected.rationale: Affective language predicts click behaviour beyond topic.

selected.name: Explanation or analysis marker
selected.instruction: Score high when the headline signals explainer or analytical framing ('Why...', 'Explaining...', 'The rise and fall'). Score low for breaking-event headlines.
selected.rationale: Explainers ride major running stories; dense model may read topic salience instead.

selected.name: Practical service promise
selected.instruction: High when the headline promises advice, instructions, or help with a decision; low when it offers no usable guidance; it does not apply without a service frame
selected.rationale: Direct utility provides an independent reason to read.

selected.name: Mystery-death hook
selected.instruction: Score high when an unexplained death or unexplained cause is the core hook ('something in room', serial killings, radiation spike). Score low when cause of harm is stated.
selected.rationale: Unresolved death mysteries are consistently among most-read items.

selected.name: Personal welfare stakes
selected.instruction: High when it signals direct effects on people’s health, safety, rights, or daily routines; low when consequences remain remote or institutional; it does not apply without individual consequences
selected.rationale: Perceived personal consequences can drive readership beyond national importance.

selected.name: Concrete Scene Vividness
selected.instruction: Scores high when the headline depicts a specific sensory scene, object, or action that is readily pictured; low when wording is abstract or bureaucratic. It does not apply when no concrete scene is conveyed.
selected.rationale: Vivid scenes are easier to imagine and remember, supporting clicks without scale or elite status.

selected.name: First-person voice
selected.instruction: Score high when the headline contains a first-person pronoun or quoted speech ('I', 'we', 'our', 'litres and litres'). Score low when it is entirely third-person institutional reporting.
selected.rationale: Personal testimony invites emotional engagement and reader clicks.

selected.name: Source Transparency
selected.instruction: Scores high when the headline identifies a source, evidence, or attribution that clarifies claim provenance; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. It does not apply to plainly observable events without contested claims.
selected.rationale: Visible sourcing can build trust and clarify why a claim merits attention.

selected.name: Ideological Polarization
selected.instruction: Scores high when opposing political, religious, national, or moral camps are identifiable; low when disagreement is technical or no stance is present. It does not apply when group positions are not explicit.
selected.rationale: Ideological stakes can mobilize readership through disagreement and identity.

selected.name: Reader-addressing question
selected.instruction: Headline is phrased as a question to the reader ("What do we know?", "How will we know...?"). Scores high; does not apply to reported questions
selected.rationale: Direct address invites the reader to click for the answer.

selected.name: POLARIZATION
selected.instruction: Scores high when the headline presents opposing camps or a divisive proposition; low when it describes consensus or a technical matter. It does not apply when disagreement is not explicitly stated
selected.rationale: Polarization increases attention by making a story socially discussable beyond listed actor and crisis categories.

selected.name: Social-Identity Resonance
selected.instruction: Scores high when the headline invokes a shared group identity, belonging, or identity-related value; low when no group identity is implicated. It does not apply when relevance requires personal details absent from the headline.
selected.rationale: Identity cues can make stories personally consequential to many readers without requiring domestic relevance.

selected.name: Scare-quoted scepticism marker
selected.instruction: Single quoted word casting doubt ('deceptive', 'unidentified', 'no value'). Scores low-to-moderate; hedge weakens urgency
selected.rationale: Hedged claims read as process news, less clickable.

selected.name: Mundane-relatable action
selected.instruction: Score high when the headline centres on an everyday, ordinary activity framed as remarkable (cutting a carrot, losing a teddy bear). Score low when actions are institutional or geopolitical.
selected.rationale: Relatable small-scale human stories draw soft-news readers.

selected.name: In-quote ordinary voice
selected.instruction: Quoted first-person speech from a non-public figure ("I cut a carrot...", "'litres and litres'") marks magazine/features commissions.
upstream_parent_all_members: Features/first-person desk, weekend scheduling, magazine-style promotion

selected.name: Follow-up headline ellipticalness
selected.instruction: Headline omits full names/events and relies on assumed prior knowledge ("Why Donald Trump lost", "The biggest news wasn't about Manafort"), signalling day 2+ of a running story.
upstream_parent_all_members: Position within a running story's lifecycle, day 2+ of coverage

selected.name: Explicit question-mark headline
selected.instruction: Headline ends in a question mark, e.g. "What do we know?" or "Did...start in...?"
selected.upstream_parent: Explainer/live-blog desk writes follow-up items on day 2+ of running stories
upstream_parent_all_members: Explainer/live-blog desk writes follow-up items on day 2+ of running stories
live page and explainer format desk

selected.name: Numerical specificity
selected.instruction: Mark digits, percentages, ages, counts, or precise quantities. This may fingerprint data-led, health, or breaking-news treatments.
upstream_parent_all_members: data, science, health, or impact-reporting desk

selected.name: Running-story recap framing
selected.instruction: Mark “what do we know,” “explaining,” “why …,” “latest images,” or similar recap language. Such wording may fingerprint a later position in a multi-day story or a designated explainer slot.

selected.name: Celebrity personal-name slot
selected.instruction: Headline leads with a bare celebrity name plus colon (Harry:, Matthew Perry:, KSI, Malala), reflecting entertainment desk conventions and promoted sidebar placement.
upstream_parent_all_members: Entertainment desk house style plus celebrity promotion slots

selected.name: Domestic-UK angle tell
selected.instruction: Explicit mention of UK, England, or a UK institution (NHS, PM), flagging the home-audience desk whose readership baseline is higher.
selected.upstream_parent: national desk promotion to domestic audience
upstream_parent_all_members: national desk promotion to domestic audience

selected.name: Leading geographic dateline
selected.instruction: Mark headlines that begin with “In” followed by a place, or with a country or city name. This can reveal foreign-desk or bureau-origin conventions.

selected.name: Quoted speech
selected.instruction: Mark headlines containing quotation marks around a phrase or sentence. Quoted headlines may fingerprint interview, reaction, or live-news formats.

selected.name: Location-heavy wording
selected.instruction: named geography | DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines containing two or more explicit countries, cities, regions, or national demonyms.
